title: Perfect-hash aggregate: per-group simple_update for few distinct groups per chunk
hypothesis: In q01 PERFECT_HASH_GROUP_BY costs 1.72s CPU over 58.8M rows (~29ns/row for 8 aggregates), second only to the scan. PerfectAggregateHashTable::AddChunk (src/execution/perfect_aggregate_hashtable.cpp:117) computes a per-row state address and calls the scatter update (AggregateExecutor::UnaryScatterLoop) once per aggregate, then VectorOperations::AddInPlace on the address vector after each aggregate. With only a handful of groups, consecutive rows hit the same state address, so every aggregate's loop is a serial read-modify-write chain through memory (store-to-load forwarding latency, no register accumulation, no vectorisation), plus 8 extra passes over the address vector. The simple_update path (UnaryFlatUpdateLoop/UnaryUpdateLoop in src/include/duckdb/common/vector_operations/aggregate_executor.hpp) takes a single __restrict state pointer, letting the compiler keep the accumulator in registers.
plan: In PerfectAggregateHashTable::AddChunk, after computing group indices (before converting to addresses), count rows per group index for this chunk. If the number of distinct groups present in the chunk is small (e.g. <= 8, and every aggregate has no filter and a non-null simple_update callback via aggregate.function.GetStateSimpleUpdateCallback()), do a stable counting-sort of row indices into one SelectionVector per present group (single pass, preserves input order within a group so order-sensitive aggregates such as first/list/string_agg and float sums give identical results). Set group_is_set for those groups. Then for each present group g and each aggregate: slice the aggregate's payload input vectors with the group's selection (Vector::Slice(vec, sel, cnt) into a temp vector, or DataChunk::Slice on a reference copy), and call simple_update(inputs, AggregateInputData(aggregate.GetFunctionData(), *aggregate_allocator), child_count, data + g*tuple_size + aggregate_offset, cnt). Count_star (child_count 0) passes nullptr inputs as UpdateStates does. Keep the bounds check / InvalidInputException for group >= total_groups. If the distinct count exceeds the threshold or any aggregate is filtered / lacks simple_update, fall back to the existing scatter path unchanged. Optionally special-case: if all rows of the chunk belong to one group, skip slicing entirely and call simple_update on the payload directly.
expected_gain: q01: aggregation CPU 1.72s -> maybe 0.8-1.0s, i.e. ~15-20% of total query CPU (~300ms -> ~250-300ms wall).
generality: Any GROUP BY on low-cardinality integer/small-domain keys that the optimizer routes to the perfect hash aggregate (flags, status codes, booleans, small enums, years) with many sum/avg/count/min/max aggregates. Queries with many distinct groups per chunk see only the cost of a per-chunk distinct count (cheap) and take the old path.
risk: Medium-low. Correctness risks: preserving order within groups (stable sort required), NULL handling (simple_update handles validity through the sliced vector's unified format), aggregates whose simple_update differs semantically from update (should not exist). Performance risk: dictionary slicing overhead per group per aggregate for chunks with ~8 groups; threshold limits it.

title: Fuse stacked projections between scan and aggregate
hypothesis: q01 has three PROJECTION operators over 58.8M rows between TABLE_SCAN and the aggregate (0.23s + 0.05s compress_string + 0.21s = ~0.5s CPU). The first computes l_extendedprice*(1-l_discount), the third recomputes #4*(1+l_tax) and re-references columns; each projection materialises vectors. Merging adjacent projections (or avoiding the compress-string projection being inserted between them) would save per-chunk overhead and copies.
plan: Investigate where the compressed-materialization optimizer (src/optimizer/compressed_materialization*) inserts the __internal_compress_string projection under an aggregate whose groups are already small, and whether a projection-merge step exists (RemoveUnusedColumns / common subexpression). Needs investigation before implementation.
generality: Any aggregate over computed expressions with string group keys.
risk: Medium; optimizer change, needs more investigation.

title: Bitpacking select: produce flat compacted vectors for filtered scans
hypothesis: In q01 the l_shipdate filter keeps about 98% of rows, but nearly every 2048-row vector loses a few. In RowGroup::Scan (src/storage/table/row_group.cpp:809-819), every non-filter column then goes through StandardColumnData::Select. Bitpacking (all 4 decimal columns: l_quantity, l_extendedprice, l_discount, l_tax) has no `select` callback; only constant, RLE and dict_fsst have one. So it falls back to ColumnData::Select, which scans the full vector and calls result.Slice(sel), so every payload column reaches the projections and the aggregate as a DICTIONARY vector. Downstream, the decimal multiplies and the aggregate scatter then take the generic sel-indirected paths instead of the flat ones. Measured with dbe-tool sql: Q1 with the filter is about 680ms. Without the filter, still scanning l_shipdate through an added max(l_shipdate), it is about 555ms, even though that version processes 2% more rows and runs an extra aggregate. Without the filter and without max it is about 480ms. So the filtered path costs at least about 18%, part of it from dictionary-sliced vectors.
plan: In src/storage/compression/bitpacking.cpp add `template <class T> void BitpackingSelect(ColumnSegment &segment, ColumnScanState &state, idx_t vector_count, Vector &result, const SelectionVector &sel, idx_t sel_count)`, matching compression_select_t in compression_function.hpp:182. It decompresses vector_count values with the existing BitpackingScanPartial<T> logic into a per-scan-state scratch buffer of STANDARD_VECTOR_SIZE T values. Add that buffer to BitpackingScanState<T> and allocate it lazily. It then gathers result_data[i] = scratch[sel.get_index(i)] for i < sel_count and leaves result as FLAT_VECTOR. Use a scratch buffer, not in-place compaction, so correctness never depends on the sel being sorted. Simplest route: call BitpackingScanPartial into a temporary Vector that wraps the scratch buffer (FlatVector::SetData), or refactor the partial scan to take a T* target. In GetBitpackingFunction set `bitpacking.select = BitpackingSelect<T>;`, keeping the ctor args unchanged, as done for get_segment_info. StandardColumnData::Select (standard_column_data.cpp:103) already routes through SelectVector when compression->select, the validity select and SCAN_ENTIRE_VECTOR are all present. Check that the validity segments of these columns (constant or uncompressed validity) have select callbacks: ConstantSelectValidity and ValiditySelect both exist. Also check that ColumnData::SelectVector's offset bookkeeping (offset_in_column += target_count) matches the bitpacking scan-state advance, which happens inside the partial scan by vector_count. Run the test/sql/storage compression tests for bitpacking.
expected_gain: q01 5-12%: projections and the perfect-hash aggregate get flat inputs. The scan pays one gather of about 2000 values per column per vector instead of creating a dictionary slice.
generality: Any filtered table scan over bitpacked integer, decimal or date columns (the default compression for most numeric data) where non-filter columns are projected, which is very common in TPC-H/DS-like workloads. Very selective filters pay a negligible gather of sel_count values. The full vector is still decompressed, as today.
risk: Low-medium. This is a storage-layer change, so correctness is the main risk: DELTA_FOR state continuity (current_delta_offset must advance over all vector_count rows, not sel_count), CONSTANT mode, hugeint/uhugeint T, and segment boundaries. The SCAN_ENTIRE_VECTOR precondition guarantees the vector lies inside one segment.

title: Perfect HT: replicate group states (K=4) to break same-state dependency chains
hypothesis: PERFECT_HASH_GROUP_BY is 1.50s CPU for 58.8M rows (~25ns/row, 8 aggregates) in profile.md. q01 has 4 groups with skew (N,O ~49%, A,F/R,F ~25% each). In RowOperations::UpdateStates -> UnaryScatter, every row of a group does a read-modify-write on the same state address, so all rows of one group form a serial chain through store-to-load forwarding (~4-6 cycles per link, longer for avg's hugeint add with carry). Out-of-order execution only overlaps the different groups, so throughput is limited by the largest group: about 0.49 x 5 cycles per row per aggregate. E0001 changed the loop structure, partitioning rows by group, and that overhead made it slower. This change keeps the existing vectorised scatter unchanged and only changes the addresses: row i goes to replica (i & 3) of its group. That splits each chain into 4 independent chains. Measured with dbe-tool sql (single runs): group by the 2 keys with count(*) alone spends 0.45s CPU in the perfect HT, so the per-row state update cost is high even for a single aggregate.
plan:
In src/execution/perfect_aggregate_hashtable.cpp and the header src/include/duckdb/execution/perfect_aggregate_hashtable.hpp:
(1) Add a member `idx_t replica_count`, set in the constructor. It is 4 when ALL aggregates have function.order_dependent == AggregateOrderDependent::NOT_ORDER_DEPENDENT, none is DISTINCT, and total_groups * tuple_size * 4 <= ~1MB (use a constant). Otherwise it is 1. Also mark avg as NOT_ORDER_DEPENDENT in extension/core_functions/aggregate/algebraic/avg.cpp (GetAverageAggregate / the decimal binder BindDecimalAvg must keep it, so set it on the returned function after the bind replaces it). avg is order-independent in the same sense sum already is.
(2) Allocate and InitializeStates for total_groups * replica_count tuples. Replica r occupies the tuple indexes [r*total_groups, (r+1)*total_groups). group_is_set keeps only total_groups entries.
(3) AddChunk: keep the group computation and the bounds check. Then set address_data[i] = data + (group + (i & (replica_count-1)) * total_groups) * tuple_size. Leave the rest unchanged (UpdateStates, AddInPlace, filtered path).
(4) Combine(other): for each set group i, and for each replica r of `other`, combine the source tuple (r*total_groups+i) into the target tuple i (the target's replica 0). Batch these into the existing source/target address vectors. Before the global table is used (Combine and Scan run on gstate.ht in physical_perfecthash_aggregate.cpp:170/196), the target's own replicas >0 must either be empty or be folded in. Simplest: the global table also receives AddChunk? Check: it does not, so it only gets Combine into replica 0. Still, add a private FoldReplicas() that combines replicas 1..K-1 into 0 for set groups. Call it at the start of Scan (once, guarded by a flag) and on `other` at the start of Combine, to be robust.
(5) Destroy(): call destructors on all total_groups*replica_count tuples whose group is set (index i % total_groups), or simply on all replicas of set groups.
expected_gain: q01: PERFECT_HASH_GROUP_BY 1.5s -> ~0.9-1.1s CPU, roughly 8-15% wall. If the chain theory is wrong, the change is neutral (extra init of 4x states, negligible).
generality: Any low-cardinality GROUP BY on small-range integer or compressed-string keys with sum/count/avg/min/max-style aggregates (the perfect HT path). The more skewed and the fewer the groups, the bigger the gain. Order-dependent aggregates (list, string_agg, first/arg_min ties) are excluded by the gate, so their results are unchanged. Possible slowdown: perfect HTs with many groups (more init and combine work); the size cap limits this.
risk: Low-medium. Correctness depends on combine being correct for all gated aggregates, which parallel execution already relies on. Floating-point sums may differ in the last bits, as they already can across threads. Make sure group_is_set and Destroy cover all replicas so there are no leaks with arena-allocated states.

title: avg on int32/int64/decimal(int64): int64 sum state when stats prove no overflow
hypothesis: PERFECT_HASH_GROUP_BY is 1.41s CPU on q01 (second-largest operator after the 2.06s scan). 3 of its 8 aggregates are avg over DECIMAL(15,2) (int64 physical). These use AvgState<hugeint_t> with AddToHugeint::AddValue (extension/core_functions/include/core_functions/aggregate/sum_helpers.hpp:109), which costs a 128-bit add, an overflow compare and a branch per row, plus a 32-byte state instead of 16 bytes. The 4 sums are already rewritten to sum_no_overflow (int64 state) by SumPropagateStats (sum.cpp:126) when |min|,|max| * max_cardinality fits int64, but avg has no such statistics callback. The same rewrite for avg turns 3 of 8 scatter loops into plain int64 adds and makes the state tuple smaller (better cache use, cheaper replicas from E0003).
plan: In extension/core_functions/aggregate/algebraic/avg.cpp: (1) add `struct IntegerAverageOperationInt64 : BaseSumOperation<AverageSetOperation, RegularAdd>` whose Finalize is bit-identical to IntegerAverageOperationHugeint: `long double divident = GetAverageDivident<long double>(count, bind_data); target = Hugeint::Cast<long double>(hugeint_t(state.value)) / divident;` (go through hugeint_t so the rounding matches exactly on every platform). (2) add `AvgPropagateStats(ClientContext&, BoundAggregateExpression &expr, AggregateStatisticsInput &input)` modelled on SumPropagateStats: require input.node_stats->has_max_cardinality and NumericStats::HasMinMax(child_stats[0]); internal type INT32 or INT64 only; compute max/min * max_cardinality in hugeint; if both are strictly inside int64 bounds, build `AggregateFunction::UnaryAggregate<AvgState<int64_t>, INPUT, double, IntegerAverageOperationInt64>(arg_type, DOUBLE)` and copy name, arguments, return type, bind callback (keep expr.bind_info untouched — the decimal scale stays), and set NOT_ORDER_DEPENDENT; clear its statistics callback; assign to expr.function. Return nullptr. (3) attach the callback (SetStatisticsCallback) to the INT32 and INT64 variants in GetAverageAggregateInternal, which also covers BindDecimalAvg for decimals with int32/int64 storage. Leave INT16 (already int64 state), INT128, interval, time types untouched. Check that a plan serialised after the rewrite (if any) still deserialises: keeping name 'avg' + bind re-run yields the hugeint version, which gives the same results.
expected_gain: q01: 3-7% (3 of 8 aggregates in the 1.41s perfect-HT operator get cheaper; state tuple shrinks by ~48 bytes).
generality: Any avg over INTEGER/BIGINT/DECIMAL(<=18) columns with min/max stats (most scans of base tables), in perfect HT, hash aggregate and ungrouped aggregate. Nothing should get slower; when stats are missing or too wide, the hugeint path is kept.
risk: Low-medium. Correctness depends on the bound check (copy the sum one exactly) and on the finalize being bit-identical (use the hugeint cast). Make sure the swapped function keeps the bind data and the result type DOUBLE.

title: Perfect HT: fused single-pass update for int64 sum/avg/count_star aggregates
hypothesis: PERFECT_HASH_GROUP_BY is still 1.32s CPU of ~2.7s query CPU on q01 (profile.md). It runs 8 aggregates x 58.8M rows = ~470M state updates, about 2.8ns each. Each aggregate takes its own pass: RowOperations::UpdateStates -> ToUnifiedFormat on a dictionary-sliced payload (the scan filter slices every column), then a scatter loop that reloads the state pointer and goes through sel indirection, and then AddInPlace on the address vector. E0001 and E0003 showed the per-pass scatter itself is the remaining cost, not dependency chains (the E0003 notes suggest fusing). A single row loop that loads the group address once and updates all the int64 states of the tuple (2 adjacent cache lines) removes 7 of the 8 address reloads, 8 AddInPlace passes and per-aggregate dispatch. The update count stays the same, but the work per update should drop by ~2x.
plan: In src/execution/perfect_aggregate_hashtable.cpp (+ .hpp): in the constructor, classify every aggregate in layout_ptr->GetAggregates(). The fused path is enabled only if ALL aggregates are unfiltered, non-distinct and one of: (a) count_star (child_count 0, state int64 counter); (b) sum_no_overflow with input physical type INT32/INT64 (state SumState<int64_t>: isset + value; check that state_size matches); (c) avg whose state is AvgState<int64_t> (from E0004: input physical INT32/INT64 and state_size == sizeof(AvgState<int64_t>) = 16; the hugeint state is larger, so state_size tells them apart; double avg must be excluded by requiring an integer physical input type). Before writing the classification, read the exact state structs in extension/core_functions/include/core_functions/aggregate/sum_helpers.hpp and avg.cpp and record the field offsets; if their layout is not reachable from src/, mirror it with static_asserted local structs. In AddChunk, after the address loop, if fused: ToUnifiedFormat each payload column once, then one loop over rows i: base = address_data[i]; for each aggregate k (small array of {kind, offset, payload col}): idx = sel_k->get_index(i); if valid, update state at base+offset_k (sum: isset=true, value+=v; avg: count++, value+=v; count_star: ++). Treat NULLs exactly as the existing ops do (sum/avg skip NULLs; count_star counts all). A templated inner loop for the case where no payload column has a validity mask is worthwhile. Otherwise use the existing per-aggregate path. Combine/Scan/finalize are unchanged because the state layouts are unchanged. Keep the E0003 replica logic.
generality: Any GROUP BY with a small group domain (perfect HT) over integer/decimal(<=18) sum/avg/count, which is very common in analytical reporting queries. Other aggregate mixes are unaffected and fall back to the existing path.
risk: Medium: mismatched state layouts would give wrong results, so use static_asserts and state_size checks. NULL handling must match. Falling back for anything unrecognised keeps the risk contained.

title: Perfect HT: replica count 8
hypothesis: E0003 K=4 cut HT CPU 1.50->1.37s. With 4 skewed groups (49% in one) and 2-cache-line tuples, 8 replicas may hide more store-to-load latency. It is cheap to try.
plan: Change MAX_REPLICA_COUNT in src/execution/perfect_aggregate_hashtable.cpp from 4 to 8, keeping the 1MiB size cap.
risk: Low; possible small slowdown for larger group domains due to cache footprint (capped).

title: Perfect HT: up to 8 replicas, largest power of two that fits the cap
hypothesis: PERFECT_HASH_GROUP_BY is still 1.13s CPU (second largest operator) for ~470M state updates. E0003 (K=4 replicas) cut 12.3% by breaking same-state read-modify-write chains. E0005 made each aggregate's update a tight typed loop, so store-to-load forwarding latency on the same state address is now a larger share of each iteration. In q01 one group holds 49% of rows: with K=4, row i and row i+4 hit the same state ~half the time, so the chain is still only 4 rows long. K=8 doubles the independent chains. Also, the current code (perfect_aggregate_hashtable.cpp:44) drops straight to replica_count=1 when total_groups*tuple_size*4 exceeds the 1MiB cap. Choosing the largest power of two that fits keeps some replication for mid-sized domains.
plan: In src/execution/perfect_aggregate_hashtable.cpp: set MAX_REPLICA_COUNT (line 10) to 8. In the constructor (~line 36-45), when can_replicate, start at MAX_REPLICA_COUNT and halve while total_groups*tuple_size*replica_count > MAX_REPLICATED_HT_SIZE and replica_count > 1. The replica mask at line 312 (replica_count-1) already assumes a power of two; keep that invariant. Check that CombineReplicas and the Scan-time fold loop over replica_count rather than a hard-coded 4 (grep for 4 or MAX_REPLICA_COUNT in the replica loops). No other changes. Bench q01 several times; if K=8 is not better than K=4 beyond noise, try K=8 with the fallback only, or report neutral.
expected_gain: q01 2-5% (HT CPU 1.13s -> ~0.95s if the chains are the remaining bottleneck).
generality: Any perfect-hash group-by with few groups and skewed or low-cardinality keys (common in reporting queries). The halving fallback also helps mid-sized group domains that currently get no replication. Possible slowdown: Init/Combine/fold costs scale with 8x states, which is negligible for tiny domains, and the extra cache footprint is bounded by the 1MiB cap.
risk: Low. The semantics are unchanged because replication is already gated on order-independent, non-DISTINCT aggregates. The only correctness hazard is a replica loop that hard-codes 4.

title: Investigate per-value cost of bitpacked int64 scans
hypothesis: Measured with EXPLAIN ANALYZE: sum(l_quantity) alone has TABLE_SCAN 0.67s CPU for 60M values (~11ns/value), sum(l_extendedprice) 1.07s (~18ns/value), and 4 bitpacked decimal columns 2.04s. The FOR bitpacking unpack (fastpforlib Unroller, 32 values per call) plus ApplyFrameOfReference should cost ~1ns/value. The overhead is either elsewhere in the scan path (ColumnData::ScanVector, GetVectorScanType, HasUpdates locks, FetchUpdates, validity scan, per-32-value dispatch in BitpackingScanPartial at bitpacking.cpp:775), or the machine's threads are oversubscribed. The wider column is slower, which suggests that the unpack or memory traffic, not fixed per-vector overhead, dominates.
plan: Investigation first: compare scan CPU of an INT64 bitpacked column with different widths, and with threads=1 vs 8, to separate machine effects from code. If unpack dominates, add an int64 fast path in BitpackingScanPartial that, for a full metadata-group-aligned FOR run, unpacks and applies the frame of reference in one fused loop over 32-value blocks (avoiding the switch dispatch per block and the second pass).
expected_gain: Unknown until measured; scan is ~60% of q01 CPU.
generality: Every scan of bitpacked integer/decimal columns.
risk: Medium; needs measurement before any code.
